title: Abu Dhabi OFW turns to cleaning toilets for a living after losing job
summary: Dubbed ‘Banyo Boy’ online, a laid-off Filipino worker in Abu Dhabi cleans toilets for AED10 to afford a new visa — sparking an outpouring of community support alongside legal warnings

blocks.text: Dubbed ‘Banyo Boy’ online, a laid-off Filipino worker in Abu Dhabi cleans toilets for AED10 to afford a new visa — sparking an outpouring of community support alongside legal warnings

items: Jaime Herrera, a 24-year-old overseas Filipino worker in the UAE, is cleaning toilets for AED10 to fund a new visa after losing his job.
Despite the illegal nature of his work during the visa grace period, he has received support from customers who pay him more and offer groceries.
His situation gained attention through a viral social media post, leading to increased demand for his cleaning services and calls for help in finding him a new job.

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates – An overseas Filipino worker (OFW) who recently lost his job has resorted to cleaning the toilets of fellow Filipinos for AED10 (P173.67) to raise funds for a new visa to stay in the country.

The good news is that 24-year-old Jaime Herrera (not his real name), who has until November 26 to legally remain in the United Arab Emirates, has been receiving numerous messages for toilet cleanups. Those he has serviced have been paying more than his asking rate and giving him groceries, he said. Others have been offering food and help finding a job.

The bad news is that under UAE law, it is illegal to engage in any form of work during a grace period after a visa has expired or been canceled unless the worker secures a new employment contract and visa.

A grace period, usually one month, only allows a foreign worker to legally remain in the country to process a status change, transition to a new employer, or exit the UAE. Working illegally during this window can result in daily overstay fines, legal action, or a reentry ban.
Herrera’s previous employment contract has been revoked.
A high school graduate, Herrera said he cannot risk becoming undocumented or flying home empty-handed.

Herrera, who hails from Dasmariñas in Cavite, has to exit to nearby Oman while a new two-month visa authorizing his stay in the UAE is processed. The entire process costs around AED4,000 – AED1,200 for the visa, and the rest for transportation and accommodation while waiting for his reentry document.
Herrera, who arrived in the UAE on July 4 this year, previously held an employment visa as a house cleaner in Dubai.
“Talagang sayang (It was really too bad),” said Herrera, adding that he was earning AED2,500 a month at that job.
He said he is currently only able to clean one toilet a day.
“Nakakapagod maglinis ng kubeta. Pero okay lang sa akin. Nagme-message sila (customers) sa akin, magko-conversation kami, ‘pag okay, kukunin ko,” Herrera shared.
“‘Yung unang customer ko, Dhs50 (P871) ang binayad sa akin, tapos binigyan ako ng mga prutas. Daming tumatawag, sa isang araw, may limang missed calls ako.”

(It’s tiring to clean a toilet, but I’m okay with that. Customers send me a message, we talk, and if it’s okay, I take the job. My first customer paid me Dhs50 and gave me some fruit. I’ve been getting lots of calls; I receive around five missed calls a day.)
Herrera said he started cleaning toilets in Abu Dhabi on October 26.

“Naghahanap ako ng trabaho. Okay naman dito. Dami kong nakikitang hiring. Nag-iipon ako ng pang-exit. Maganda rin dito sa UAE, pumalpak lang ang mga plano ko. Unang sahod ko, bumili ako ng scooter, naibenta rin, sayang,” he said.

(I’m looking for a job. It’s okay here. I see a lot of hiring. I’m saving up for my exit. Life is good here in the UAE; my plans just went wrong. I bought a scooter with my first paycheck, but I ended up selling it — what a waste.)
Herrera became the talk of the town when a vlogger, Mercy Dimalanta (not her real name), came across his social media post offering toilet-cleaning services and shared it on her Facebook account.

“(K)ung may labis naman po kayong budget, ibigay ‘nyo na po ang paglilinis ng CR ‘nyo sa kanya dahil napakalaking tulong po sa kanya ang AED10 para makatawid siya sa araw-araw niyang pamumuhay dito sa Abu Dhabi. Higit na marangal ang ginagawa niya kumpara sa ginagawa ng iba. Noong nakita ko ang post niya, alam ko na kailangang-kailangan niya ng tulong kaya agad akong nag-message at ang bilis niyang nag-reply, patunay na abang na abang siya sa kung sinuman ang gusto magpalinis upang may pagkunan siya ng pagkain niya sa araw na ‘yun,” she wrote on Facebook.

(If you happen to have some extra budget, please consider hiring him to clean your bathroom; the AED10 would be a huge help for his daily survival here in Abu Dhabi. The work he does is far more honorable than what some others might resort to. When I saw his post, I knew he was in desperate need of help, so I reached out immediately. He replied right away — proof that he is eagerly waiting for anyone who might need cleaning services, just so he can afford a meal for the day.)
Dimalanta gave him the moniker “Banyo Boy.” And Herrera’s sudden influx of customer calls is largely attributed to her viral Facebook post.
“Tumutulo ang luha ko sa awa pero lamang ang paghanga. Kaya naman pagkatapos niyang maglinis, ibinigay ko ang bayad ko lakip ang munting grocery na dapat sana ay para sa amin,” she added.
“Naitanong ko rin kung may trabaho ba siya at sabi niya ay wala, kaya bukod sa pagpapalinis ng CR ‘nyo, inilalapit ko rin po na sana tulungan natin siya magkaroon ng trabaho.”

(Tears streamed down my face out of pity, but my admiration for him was even greater. So, after he finished cleaning, I handed him my payment, along with some small grocery items that were supposed to be for us. I also asked if he had a job, and he said he didn’t; so, aside from having him clean your bathrooms, I’m also appealing to everyone to help him find a job.) – Rappler.com
